subject: Mathematics
title: The Great Festival Money Trail
hook: Priya saves money for Diwali in a growing pattern—discover the hidden math in daily decisions.

slides.title: Sequences and Series: The Festival Money Trail
slides.storyContext: Priya's grandmother challenges her: save for Diwali gifts using a special rule. Each day you get money that follows a pattern.
slides.inSimpleWords: Numbers arranged in a special order, one after another, following a rule.

slides.title: The Diwali Savings Challenge
slides.storyContext: It's July. Priya's grandmother says: 'On day 1, I give you ₹2. On day 2, ₹4. On day 3, ₹8. Keep going until Diwali in October. Can you predict how much you'll have?' Priya starts writing: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32... Grandfather smiles and says, 'You've found a sequence. Now let's master its mathematics.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A sequence is a list of numbers arranged in order following a pattern.

slides.title: What is a Sequence?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A sequence is a set of numbers arranged in a definite order, following a rule. Denoted a₁, a₂, a₃, ..., aₙ.

points.label: Arithmetic Sequence (AP)
points.text: Each term differs from the previous by a constant d (common difference). Example: 5, 10, 15, 20, ... has d = 5.

points.label: General Term (AP)
points.text: aₙ = a₁ + (n-1)d, where a₁ is the first term and d is the common difference.

example.problem: In a school, chairs are arranged for an assembly. Row 1 has 12 chairs, Row 2 has 14 chairs, Row 3 has 16 chairs. What is the 10th row?
example.solution: This is an AP: a₁ = 12, d = 2. Using aₙ = a₁ + (n-1)d, a₁₀ = 12 + (10-1)×2 = 12 + 18 = 30 chairs.

slides.inSimpleWords: In arithmetic sequences, you add the same number every time.

slides.title: Geometric Sequences—The Doubling Rule

points.label: Geometric Sequence (GP)
points.text: Each term is multiplied by a constant r (common ratio). Example: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 has r = 2.

points.label: General Term (GP)
points.text: aₙ = a₁ × r^(n-1), where a₁ is the first term and r is the common ratio.

points.label: Priya's Savings
points.text: Day 1: ₹2, Day 2: ₹4, Day 3: ₹8. This is a GP with a₁ = 2, r = 2. By day 10: a₁₀ = 2 × 2^(10-1) = 2 × 512 = ₹1024.

example.problem: A rice farmer doubles his stock every month. He starts with 10 kg. How much will he have in 6 months?

slides.inSimpleWords: In geometric sequences, you multiply by the same number every time—things grow fast!

slides.title: Sum of an Arithmetic Series

points.label: Series
points.text: The sum of the terms of a sequence. If we add up the sequence 5, 10, 15, 20, we get a series.

points.label: Sum Formula (AP)
points.text: Sₙ = n/2 × (2a₁ + (n-1)d) or Sₙ = n/2 × (a₁ + aₙ), where n is the number of terms.

points.label: Real Example
points.text: A builder stacks pipes: row 1 has 5 pipes, row 2 has 7 pipes, row 3 has 9 pipes. Find total pipes in 10 rows.

example.problem: Row 1: 5 pipes, Row 2: 7, Row 3: 9 (AP with a₁ = 5, d = 2). Sum of 10 rows?

slides.inSimpleWords: To add up an arithmetic sequence, use the average of first and last term times the count.

slides.title: Sum of a Geometric Series

points.label: Finite GP Sum
points.text: Sₙ = a₁(r^n - 1)/(r - 1) when r ≠ 1. For Priya's doubling money: S₁₀ = 2(2^10 - 1)/(2-1) = 2(1024-1) = ₹2046.

points.label: Real Life
points.text: A city's population grows 5% yearly. After many years, what's the total cumulative growth? Use GP sum formulas.

example.problem: Priya's daily Diwali savings double each day for 5 days (₹2, ₹4, ₹8, ₹16, ₹32). Total savings?

slides.inSimpleWords: Geometric series sums grow exponentially—useful for money, populations, and viral spread.

slides.title: Full Problem: Kumar's Cricket Score Streak
slides.storyContext: Kumar scores in a cricket tournament: Match 1: 15 runs, Match 2: 20 runs, Match 3: 25 runs (increasing by 5 each match). He plays 12 matches. What is his total score?

points.label: Identify
points.text: Arithmetic sequence: a₁ = 15, d = 5, n = 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the AP sum formula when you know first term, difference, and number of terms.

slides.title: Your Challenge: The Rice Granary
slides.storyContext: A farmer stores rice in bags. The 1st day he stores 100 kg, the 2nd day 200 kg, the 3rd day 300 kg. After 20 days, how much rice has he stored in total? (Hint: it's an AP.)

example.problem: Find the total rice stored over 20 days where day n stores 100n kg.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sequences and series help predict totals in real work: production, savings, growth.

slides.title: Sequences & Series Summary

points.text: Sequence: ordered list of numbers following a rule (a₁, a₂, a₃, ...).
Arithmetic Sequence: constant difference d; aₙ = a₁ + (n-1)d; Sₙ = n/2 × (a₁ + aₙ).
Geometric Sequence: constant ratio r; aₙ = a₁ × r^(n-1); Sₙ = a₁(r^n-1)/(r-1).
Use AP for linear growth (stairs, rows, daily increases). Use GP for exponential growth (doubling, viral spread).
Master both to solve real problems: harvests, savings, cricket scores, crowd sizes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sequences organize data; series sum them up. Both are tools for predicting and planning.

subject: Mathematics
title: The Village Path Blueprint
hook: A surveyor maps village paths—learn the math behind straight lines and angles.

characters.name: Meena
characters.role: Local farmer interested in land division

slides.title: Straight Lines: Mapping the Village Path
slides.storyContext: Surveyor Sharma must map new paths between the village well (at 2,3) and the temple (at 8,9) on a coordinate grid. Arjun asks: how do we describe this path mathematically?
slides.inSimpleWords: A straight line on a coordinate plane can be described with equations and slopes.

slides.title: The Well and the Temple
slides.storyContext: Arjun holds the surveyor's chain as Surveyor Sharma plots coordinates. 'The well is at grid (2,3). The temple is at (8,9),' Sharma explains. 'To find the path, we need to know the direction—how steep is the climb? And where does the path cross the well's baseline?' Arjun sketches on paper. 'Is there a formula?' Sharma nods. 'Yes—we call it the slope-intercept form.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Every straight line has a slope (steepness) and a y-intercept (where it crosses the y-axis).

slides.title: Slope of a Line

points.label: Definition
points.text: Slope m = (y₂ - y₁)/(x₂ - x₁). It measures how steep a line is.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: m > 0: line rises (northeast). m < 0: line falls (southeast). m = 0: horizontal. m undefined: vertical.

points.label: Well to Temple
points.text: Points (2,3) and (8,9). Slope m = (9-3)/(8-2) = 6/6 = 1. The path rises at a 45° angle.

example.problem: A farmer walks from point (1,2) to point (4,8). What is the slope of the path?
example.solution: m = (8-2)/(4-1) = 6/3 = 2. The path rises 2 units for every 1 unit walked horizontally.

slides.inSimpleWords: Slope tells you how fast a line rises or falls—steeper slope means a sharper climb.

slides.title: Equation of a Line: Slope-Intercept Form

points.label: Form
points.text: y = mx + c, where m is slope and c is the y-intercept (where line crosses y-axis).

points.label: Finding c
points.text: Using the well-temple line: slope m = 1, point (2,3). Substitute: 3 = 1(2) + c → c = 1.

points.label: Final Equation
points.text: The path line is y = x + 1. Any point (x,y) on this path satisfies this equation.

example.problem: A road passes through (3,5) with slope 2. Find its equation.
example.solution: y = mx + c. Using (3,5): 5 = 2(3) + c → c = -1. Equation: y = 2x - 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: The equation y = mx + c is the universal formula for any straight line.

slides.title: Two-Point Form and General Form

points.label: Two-Point Form
points.text: (y - y₁)/(x - x₁) = (y₂ - y₁)/(x₂ - x₁). Use this when you have two points.

points.label: General Form
points.text: Ax + By + C = 0. Example: x - y + 1 = 0 is the well-temple line rearranged.

points.label: Intercept Form
points.text: x/a + y/b = 1, where a is x-intercept and b is y-intercept. Useful for axes crossings.

example.problem: Write the equation of the line through (0,4) and (2,0).
example.solution: Intercept form: x/2 + y/4 = 1, or 2x + y = 4. General form: 2x + y - 4 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different forms of line equations serve different situations—pick the form that fits your data.

slides.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines

points.label: Parallel Lines
points.text: Two lines are parallel if they have the same slope: m₁ = m₂. They never meet.

points.label: Perpendicular Lines
points.text: Two lines are perpendicular if m₁ × m₂ = -1. Example: if m₁ = 2, then m₂ = -1/2.

points.label: Village Application
points.text: The path y = x + 1 is perpendicular to y = -x + 5 (slopes: 1 and -1, product = -1).

example.problem: Find a line parallel to y = 3x + 2 passing through (1,5).
example.solution: Parallel means same slope m = 3. Using y = 3x + c: 5 = 3(1) + c → c = 2. Answer: y = 3x + 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines have same slope; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is -1.

slides.title: Distance from a Point to a Line

points.label: Distance Formula
points.text: Distance from point (x₀,y₀) to line Ax + By + C = 0 is d = |Ax₀ + By₀ + C|/√(A² + B²).

points.label: Use Case
points.text: How far is Meena's farm at (5,7) from the path-line x - y + 1 = 0?

example.problem: Find the distance from (2,3) to the line 3x + 4y - 5 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance formula helps measure shortest separation between a point and a line.

slides.title: Full Problem: Mapping Two Farm Boundaries
slides.storyContext: Surveyor Sharma must find where two farm boundaries meet. Farm A's edge: y = 2x + 3. Farm B's edge: y = -x + 9. Where do they intersect?

points.label: Set Equal
points.text: At intersection, y values are equal: 2x + 3 = -x + 9.

points.label: Find y
points.text: y = 2(2) + 3 = 7. Intersection at (2,7).

slides.inSimpleWords: To find where two lines meet, solve their equations simultaneously.

slides.title: Your Challenge: The Water Channel
slides.storyContext: The village needs a water channel perpendicular to the main path (y = 2x + 1) passing through the well at (2,3). Write the equation of the channel.

example.problem: Find a line perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 through (2,3).
example.solution: Perpendicular slope: m₁ × m₂ = -1 → 2 × m₂ = -1 → m₂ = -1/2. Using (2,3): 3 = (-1/2)(2) + c → c = 4. Equation: y = -x/2 + 4 or x + 2y - 8 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use slope relationships to design perpendicular structures—paths, drains, and boundaries.

slides.title: Straight Lines Summary

points.text: Slope m = Δy/Δx. It measures line steepness and direction.
Equations: y = mx + c (slope-intercept), Ax + By + C = 0 (general), x/a + y/b = 1 (intercept).
Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes with product -1.
Distance from point to line: d = |Ax₀ + By₀ + C|/√(A² + B²).
Applications: surveying lands, designing roads, planning buildings, farm boundaries.

slides.inSimpleWords: Straight line equations are the foundation of coordinate geometry—used in architecture, surveying, and engineering.

subject: Mathematics
title: The Mirror and the Curve
hook: A satellite dish, a bridge arch, and a planet's orbit—all follow conic section curves.

slides.title: Conic Sections: Circles, Ellipses, Parabolas, Hyperbolas
slides.storyContext: When light rays are cut by a cone at different angles, they create curves used everywhere: satellite dishes, bridge arches, planets' orbits, and water fountains.
slides.inSimpleWords: Conic sections are curves made by slicing a cone—each has unique properties and equations.

slides.title: The Fountain Challenge
slides.storyContext: Govind is designing a water fountain for the village square. The water jets must follow a perfect arch—not too steep, not too flat. Ravi says, 'That's a parabola!' Govind nods: 'Yes, and I need its equation to calculate flow rates.' Diya adds, 'Parabolas appear in satellites too—they focus signals to a receiver.' All three realize conics are everywhere.
slides.inSimpleWords: Conic sections model real-world curves from engineering to astronomy.

slides.title: Circle: The Perfect Curve

points.label: Definition
points.text: A circle is the set of all points equidistant from a center. Distance = radius r.

points.label: Standard Equation
points.text: (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r², where (h,k) is center and r is radius.

points.label: General Equation
points.text: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0. Center = (-g, -f), radius = √(g² + f² - c).

example.problem: A circular well has center at (2,3) and radius 5. Write its equation.

slides.inSimpleWords: A circle is defined by one center point and a radius—the simplest conic section.

slides.title: Parabola: The Arch of Motion

points.label: Definition
points.text: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from a focus F and a directrix line.

points.label: Standard Equation (Vertex at origin)
points.text: y² = 4ax (opens right) or x² = 4ay (opens up). Here a is distance from vertex to focus.

points.label: Fountain Example
points.text: Water jet equation x² = 4(1.25)y = 5y. Focus at (0, 1.25), directrix at y = -1.25.

example.problem: A water fountain parabola is x² = 8y. Find focus and directrix.
example.solution: 4a = 8 → a = 2. Focus at (0, 2). Directrix: y = -2. Water rises symmetrically from the center.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parabolas are perfect arches used in water fountains, bridge cables, and satellite dishes.

slides.title: Ellipse: The Stretched Circle

points.label: Definition
points.text: An ellipse is the set of points where sum of distances to two foci = constant (2a).

points.label: Standard Equation
points.text: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a ≥ b). Semi-major axis = a, semi-minor axis = b.

points.label: Foci and Eccentricity
points.text: Foci at (±c, 0) where c² = a² - b². Eccentricity e = c/a (0 < e < 1).

example.problem: A planet's orbit is x²/100 + y²/64 = 1 (in million km). Find semi-major axis, semi-minor axis, and foci.
example.solution: a = 10, b = 8. c² = 100 - 64 = 36 → c = 6. Foci at (±6, 0). Semi-major = 10, semi-minor = 8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ellipses describe planetary orbits and stretched circular paths—essential to astronomy.

slides.title: Hyperbola: The Twin Curves

points.label: Definition
points.text: A hyperbola is the set of points where |difference of distances| to two foci = constant (2a).

points.label: Standard Equation
points.text: x²/a² - y²/b² = 1 (opens left-right). Foci at (±c, 0) where c² = a² + b².

points.label: Asymptotes
points.text: Lines y = ±(b/a)x. Hyperbola approaches these lines but never crosses.

example.problem: Write the equation of a hyperbola with foci at (±5, 0) and difference of distances = 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hyperbolas are two mirrored curves that approach asymptotes—used in radar and navigation.

slides.title: Real-World Applications of Conics

points.label: Parabola
points.text: Satellite dishes, water fountains, bridge arches, projectile motion (cricket ball trajectory).

points.label: Ellipse
points.text: Planetary orbits (Kepler's 1st law), whispering galleries (sound focuses), swimming pools.

points.label: Hyperbola
points.text: Radio towers (hyperbolic reflectors), GPS systems, nuclear cooling towers.

points.label: Circle
points.text: Wheels, orbits (special case of ellipse), architectural designs, wheels on carts.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every conic section solves real problems—from designing buildings to tracking satellites.

slides.title: Full Problem: The Bridge Arch
slides.storyContext: An engineer designs a bridge with a parabolic arch. The arch spans 40 meters horizontally and rises 10 meters at the center. Write the equation.

points.label: Set up coordinates
points.text: Vertex at origin (0,0). Left end at (-20,-10), right end at (20,-10). Opening downward: x² = -4ay.

points.label: Equation
points.text: x² = -40y or y = -x²/40. This describes the bridge's perfect arch.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real bridge arches are parabolas—calculated to support weight evenly across the span.

slides.title: Your Challenge: The Satellite Dish
slides.storyContext: A satellite receiver is designed as a parabolic mirror y² = 16x. A signal receiver sits at the focus. Find the focus coordinates.

example.problem: For the parabola y² = 16x, find the focus.
example.solution: Form y² = 4ax. Here 4a = 16 → a = 4. Focus at (4, 0). All signals parallel to the axis reflect to this point.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parabolic mirrors focus parallel rays to a single point—the key to powerful receivers.

slides.title: Conic Sections Summary

points.text: Circle: (x-h)² + (y-k)² = r². All points equidistant from center.
Parabola: y² = 4ax or x² = 4ay. Equidistant from focus and directrix. Used in dishes, fountains, arches.
Ellipse: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1. Sum of distances to foci is constant. Describes planetary orbits.
Hyperbola: x²/a² - y²/b² = 1. Difference of distances to foci is constant. Used in navigation.
Every conic has eccentricity e: circle (e=0), ellipse (0<e<1), parabola (e=1), hyperbola (e>1).

slides.inSimpleWords: Conic sections are the foundation of orbital mechanics, optics, and architectural design.

subject: Mathematics
title: Building in Three Dimensions
hook: From flat paper to real buildings—learn to navigate and measure in 3D space.

slides.title: 3D Geometry: Building in Three Dimensions
slides.storyContext: Architect Patel must design a new school building. The design requires coordinates in 3D: length, width, and height. Ankit asks, 'How do we describe positions in 3D space?'
slides.inSimpleWords: In 3D space, every point needs three coordinates (x, y, z)—length, width, and height.

slides.title: From 2D Drawings to 3D Reality
slides.storyContext: Ankit holds the architect's blueprint. 'On the drawing, the door is at (2,3)—that's flat,' says Patel. 'But in the real building, we must say (2,3,0) for ground level, or (2,3,1.5) if it's on the wall. We need a third coordinate for height.' Priya sketches: 'So (x,y,z) describes any point in the building?' Patel nods. 'Exactly. Let's master 3D coordinates.'
slides.inSimpleWords: The 3D coordinate system extends 2D coordinates by adding height as the z-axis.

slides.title: The 3D Coordinate System

points.label: Three Axes
points.text: x-axis (length), y-axis (width), z-axis (height). They meet at origin O(0,0,0).

points.label: Octants
points.text: 3D space divides into 8 octants, like quadrants in 2D but in 3D.

points.label: Point Representation
points.text: Any point P in 3D is (x, y, z). Example: a door handle at (2, 3, 1.8) meters.

example.problem: Locate the corner of a room at (4, 6, 0). What is its position relative to the origin?
example.solution: 4 meters along x-axis, 6 meters along y-axis, ground level (z=0). This is where a wall meets another wall on the floor.

slides.inSimpleWords: The 3D coordinate system uses three perpendicular axes to locate any point in space.

slides.title: Distance Between Two Points in 3D

points.label: Distance Formula
points.text: Distance AB = √((x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)² + (z₂-z₁)²)

points.label: Building Application
points.text: From ground door (2,3,0) to roof corner (5,8,10), distance = √((5-2)² + (8-3)² + (10-0)²) = √(9+25+100) = √134 ≈ 11.6 meters.

points.label: Pythagoras in 3D
points.text: The formula extends Pythagorean theorem to three dimensions.

example.problem: Find the distance from room corner (1,2,3) to ceiling point (4,6,5).

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D distance formula is like the 2D Pythagorean theorem, but with a third dimension added.

slides.title: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios

points.label: Direction Ratios
points.text: For vector from A(x₁,y₁,z₁) to B(x₂,y₂,z₂): direction ratios are (a,b,c) = (x₂-x₁, y₂-y₁, z₂-z₁).

points.label: Direction Cosines
points.text: l = a/d, m = b/d, n = c/d, where d = √(a²+b²+c²) is the distance. Note: l² + m² + n² = 1.

points.label: Building Example
points.text: From (2,3,0) to (5,8,10), ratios are (3,5,10). Distance d = √134. Cosines: l≈0.26, m≈0.43, n≈0.87.

example.problem: Find direction cosines from A(0,0,0) to B(1,1,1).
example.solution: Ratios: (1,1,1). Distance: √3. Cosines: l = 1/√3, m = 1/√3, n = 1/√3. Each ≈ 0.577.

slides.inSimpleWords: Direction cosines describe how a line is oriented in 3D space—useful for architectural slopes.

slides.title: Section Formula: Dividing a Line Segment

points.label: Internal Division
points.text: Point P divides line AB in ratio m:n. Then P = ((m·x₂ + n·x₁)/(m+n), (m·y₂ + n·y₁)/(m+n), (m·z₂ + n·z₁)/(m+n)).

points.label: Midpoint (1:1 ratio)
points.text: Midpoint M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2, (z₁+z₂)/2).

points.label: Application
points.text: Architects use this to locate structural supports: if a beam runs from (0,0,0) to (10,10,10), support at 2:1 point is at (20/3, 20/3, 20/3) ≈ (6.67, 6.67, 6.67).

example.problem: Find point P dividing segment from A(1,2,3) to B(7,8,9) in ratio 2:1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Section formula helps locate structural points along beams and construction lines.

slides.title: Equation of a Line in 3D

points.label: Parametric Form
points.text: Line through point A(a,b,c) with direction (l,m,n): x = a + lt, y = b + mt, z = c + nt, where t is parameter.

points.label: Wall Edge Example
points.text: Wall edge from (0,0,0) to (0,5,3) has parametric: x=0, y=5t, z=3t. At t=0: (0,0,0); at t=1: (0,5,3).

example.problem: Write parametric equations for a line through (2,3,4) with direction (1,2,3).

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D line equations use parameters (t) to describe every point along the line.

slides.title: Full Problem: The Diagonal Beam
slides.storyContext: Architect Patel designs a diagonal support beam from corner A(0,0,0) to opposite corner B(10,8,6) of a building. Find the beam's length and the point exactly halfway along.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The beam is 14.14 meters long. The midpoint (5,4,3) is where the architect plans a structural support.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D distance and section formulas are essential for structural engineering and construction planning.

slides.title: Your Challenge: The Rooftop Antenna
slides.storyContext: An antenna is placed at (5, 4, 12)—on the roof corner at height 12m. The base of the antenna pole is at (5, 4, 0). Find the antenna's length and direction cosines.

example.problem: From (5,4,0) to (5,4,12), find length and direction cosines.
example.solution: Length: √((5-5)² + (4-4)² + (12-0)²) = √144 = 12 meters. Direction ratios: (0,0,12). Direction cosines: l=0, m=0, n=1 (points straight up).

slides.inSimpleWords: Vertical structures like antennas have simple direction cosines—all the cosine goes to n.

slides.title: 3D Geometry Summary

points.text: 3D coordinates (x,y,z) locate points in space using three perpendicular axes.
Distance: d = √((x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)² + (z₂-z₁)²).
Direction cosines (l,m,n) describe line orientation; l² + m² + n² = 1.
Section formula divides a segment in any ratio; midpoint is the 1:1 case.
Line in 3D: parametric form (x,y,z) = (a,b,c) + t(l,m,n) or symmetric form.
Applications: architecture, construction, surveying, navigation, computer graphics.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D geometry extends 2D coordinate ideas to the real world—essential for building and design.

subject: Mathematics
title: The Instantaneous Speed
hook: How fast is a cricket ball moving at one instant? Limits and derivatives unlock the secret.

slides.title: Limits and Derivatives: The Math of Instant Change
slides.storyContext: Rohan watches the cricket match. A bowler delivers at 140 km/h—but how do we define speed at ONE instant, not over a distance?
slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives measure instantaneous rates of change—how fast something is changing at this very moment.

slides.title: The Bowler's Speed
slides.storyContext: Coach Kumar explains to Rohan: 'Average speed is distance/time over a distance. But a radar gun measures speed at ONE instant—the ball's velocity now. That's where calculus comes in.' Aisha adds, 'We use limits to shrink the time interval to zero, then we get the derivative.' Coach nods: 'Exactly. Let me teach you both.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Average speed over time versus instantaneous speed at a single moment—derivatives bridge the gap.

slides.title: Limits: Approaching a Value

points.label: Definition
points.text: lim(x→a) f(x) = L means as x gets closer to a, f(x) gets closer to L.

points.label: Ball Distance
points.text: Distance traveled: s(t) = 5t². As time t → 1, what is s(t)? s(1) = 5, s(0.9) = 4.05, s(0.99) = 4.9005. Limit is 5.

points.label: Left and Right Limits
points.text: lim(x→a⁻) = left limit, lim(x→a⁺) = right limit. If both equal L, the limit exists.

example.problem: Find lim(x→2) (x² + 3x - 1).

slides.inSimpleWords: A limit is the value a function approaches as the input gets closer to a specific number.

slides.title: Continuity at a Point

points.label: Definition
points.text: f is continuous at x = a if lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).

points.label: Three Conditions
points.text: (1) f(a) exists, (2) lim(x→a) f(x) exists, (3) both are equal.

points.label: Real Example
points.text: A cricket ball's height as it flies—continuous unless it gets caught. A function with a hole or jump is discontinuous.

example.problem: Is f(x) = (x² - 4)/(x - 2) continuous at x = 2?
example.solution: f(2) is undefined (0/0). But lim(x→2) (x² - 4)/(x - 2) = lim(x→2) (x + 2) = 4. The function has a removable discontinuity at x = 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Continuous functions have no breaks, holes, or jumps—they graph as smooth, unbroken curves.

slides.title: The Derivative: Instantaneous Rate of Change

points.label: Definition
points.text: Derivative f'(a) = lim(h→0) [f(a+h) - f(a)]/h. It is the slope of the tangent at x = a.

points.label: Geometric Meaning
points.text: The slope of the tangent line to the curve at a point. For straight lines, it is the slope m.

points.label: Ball Velocity
points.text: Distance s(t) = 5t². Velocity = ds/dt = lim(h→0) [5(t+h)² - 5t²]/h = 10t. At t=1, velocity = 10 m/s.

example.problem: Find the derivative of f(x) = x² at x = 3 using the definition.

slides.inSimpleWords: The derivative at a point is the slope of the tangent line—it tells how fast the function is changing.

slides.title: Derivative Rules: Power, Product, Chain

points.label: Power Rule
points.text: If f(x) = xⁿ, then f'(x) = n·x^(n-1). Example: f(x) = x³ → f'(x) = 3x².

points.label: Chain Rule
points.text: [f(g(x))]' = f'(g(x))·g'(x). Used for composite functions.

example.problem: Find derivative of f(x) = 3x⁴ - 2x² + 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative rules let you find rates of change quickly without using limits every time.

slides.title: Physical Interpretation: Velocity and Acceleration

points.label: Velocity
points.text: v(t) = ds/dt, where s is position. It is the first derivative of position.

points.label: Acceleration
points.text: a(t) = dv/dt, where v is velocity. It is the second derivative of position.

points.label: Cricket Ball
points.text: If s(t) = 5t² (position in meters), then v(t) = 10t (velocity), a(t) = 10 (constant acceleration = 10 m/s²).

example.problem: A car's position is s(t) = 2t³ + t². Find velocity and acceleration at t = 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Velocity is the rate of position change; acceleration is the rate of velocity change—both are derivatives.

slides.title: Full Problem: The Bowler's Delivery
slides.storyContext: A fast bowler's hand (with ball) position during delivery is s(t) = 10t² - 2t + 1 meters. What is the ball's velocity and acceleration at t = 0.5 seconds?

points.label: Acceleration
points.text: a(t) = dv/dt = 20 m/s² (constant).

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: At release (t=0.5s), the ball moves at 8 m/s and accelerates at constant 20 m/s² due to the bowler's arm motion.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives of position give velocity; derivatives of velocity give acceleration—the chain of motion.

slides.title: Your Challenge: The Pendulum Swing
slides.storyContext: A pendulum's angle is θ(t) = 0.5 sin(2t) radians. Find its angular velocity at t = π/4.

example.problem: Find dθ/dt for θ(t) = 0.5 sin(2t), then evaluate at t = π/4.
example.solution: dθ/dt = 0.5 × cos(2t) × 2 = cos(2t). At t = π/4: dθ/dt = cos(π/2) = 0 rad/s. (The pendulum momentarily stops at the highest point.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives of trigonometric functions describe oscillating motion—useful for pendulums, waves, and vibrations.

slides.title: Limits and Derivatives Summary

points.text: Limit: lim(x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) approaches L as x approaches a.
Continuity: f is continuous at a if lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).
Derivative: f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) - f(x)]/h. Slope of tangent line at x.
Power Rule: d/dx[xⁿ] = n·x^(n-1). Chain Rule: d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x).
Velocity = ds/dt (first derivative). Acceleration = d²s/dt² (second derivative).
Derivatives are the foundation of calculus—used in physics, engineering, economics, and motion analysis.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives measure how fast things change instantaneously—the core concept of differential calculus.

subject: Mathematics
title: Understanding Data: The Village Health Survey
hook: A health worker surveys the village—learn to organize, analyze, and interpret data.

characters.name: Vikram
characters.role: Farmer providing data on crops and health

slides.title: Statistics: Understanding Data from the Village
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma conducts a health survey of 100 villagers. Neha helps record heights, weights, and ages. Can they find patterns and predict health trends?
slides.inSimpleWords: Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, and interpreting data to find patterns.

slides.title: The Health Survey Begins
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma measures heights of 100 children: 120, 125, 130, 128, ... Neha writes them down. 'How do we find the typical height? How spread out are the heights?' she asks. Dr. Sharma smiles: 'That's statistics. We calculate mean, median, and standard deviation.' Vikram joins: 'How do we show this data clearly?' Neha says, 'With histograms and frequency tables!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Organize raw data into tables and graphs to reveal patterns and averages.

slides.title: Measures of Central Tendency: Mean, Median, Mode

points.label: Mean (Average)
points.text: Mean = Σx / n, where Σx is sum of all values and n is count. Heights: 120, 125, 130, 128, 132 → Mean = (120+125+130+128+132)/5 = 635/5 = 127 cm.

points.label: Median
points.text: Middle value when data is sorted. For 5 values: 120, 125, 128, 130, 132 → Median = 128 (3rd value).

points.label: Mode
points.text: Most frequent value. If heights 128, 130, 128, 128 appear most, Mode = 128.

example.problem: 10 students' test scores: 65, 78, 82, 78, 90, 78, 85, 92, 88, 95. Find mean, median, and mode.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean is the average, median is the middle value, mode is the most common value.

slides.title: Measures of Dispersion: Range, Variance, Standard Deviation

points.label: Range
points.text: Range = Maximum - Minimum. Heights: 120 to 132 → Range = 132 - 120 = 12 cm.

points.label: Variance
points.text: Variance σ² = Σ(x - mean)² / n. Measures how spread out data is from the mean.

points.label: Standard Deviation
points.text: σ = √(variance). It is the 'average deviation' from the mean. Lower σ = data is tightly clustered; higher σ = data is spread out.

example.problem: Heights 120, 125, 130, 128, 132. Mean = 127. Find variance and standard deviation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Variance and standard deviation measure how spread out data is—useful for assessing consistency.

slides.title: Frequency Distribution and Histograms

points.label: Frequency Table
points.text: Organize data into classes. Heights 120-125: 5 children, 125-130: 12 children, 130-135: 8 children.

points.label: Histogram
points.text: Bar graph where height of bar = frequency. Width = class width (constant). Used for continuous data.

points.label: Frequency Polygon
points.text: Line graph connecting midpoints of histogram bars. Shows trend in data.

example.problem: 100 children's heights grouped: 120-125 (15), 125-130 (35), 130-135 (30), 135-140 (20). Sketch the histogram.
example.solution: x-axis: height ranges. y-axis: frequency. Bars at heights 15, 35, 30, 20 respectively. Tallest bar is 125-130 range (35 children).

slides.inSimpleWords: Frequency tables and histograms organize large datasets into visual patterns.

slides.title: Cumulative Frequency and Quartiles

points.label: Cumulative Frequency
points.text: Running total of frequencies. Heights: 120-125 (5), then 125-130 (5+12=17), then 130-135 (17+8=25), etc.

points.label: Quartiles
points.text: Q₁ (25th percentile), Q₂ (median, 50th), Q₃ (75th). Divide sorted data into 4 equal parts.

points.label: Interquartile Range
points.text: IQR = Q₃ - Q₁. Measures middle 50% spread of data.

example.problem: For 100 children sorted by height, find Q₁ and Q₃. Q₁ is at position 25.5, Q₃ at 75.5.
example.solution: If sorted heights at position 25.5 is 127 cm, then Q₁ = 127. If at position 75.5 is 135 cm, then Q₃ = 135. IQR = 135 - 127 = 8 cm.

slides.inSimpleWords: Quartiles divide data into quarters—useful for understanding how data is distributed.

slides.title: Correlation and Regression (Introduction)

points.label: Correlation
points.text: Measures strength of linear relationship between two variables. Correlation coefficient r ranges from -1 to +1.

points.label: r = +1
points.text: Perfect positive correlation: as one increases, other increases.

points.label: r = -1
points.text: Perfect negative correlation: as one increases, other decreases.

points.label: r = 0
points.text: No linear correlation. Example: child height vs. test score (weak).

example.problem: A study shows age vs. income for 50 workers. Calculate correlation to see relationship strength.
example.solution: Using formula or tools, if r = 0.75, there is strong positive correlation (older workers tend to earn more).

slides.inSimpleWords: Correlation measures how two variables change together—positive (both up), negative (opposite), or zero (no link).

slides.title: Full Problem: Analyzing Crop Yields
slides.storyContext: Vikram records maize yields (in quintals) from 10 farms: 15, 18, 20, 22, 17, 21, 19, 23, 20, 18. Analyze the data.

points.label: Mean
points.text: Sum = 193. Mean = 193/10 = 19.3 quintals.

points.label: Median
points.text: Middle values are 19 and 20. Median = (19+20)/2 = 19.5 quintals.

points.label: Range
points.text: 23 - 15 = 8 quintals.

slides.inSimpleWords: Statistical analysis reveals farm yield patterns—useful for predicting future harvests and planning.

slides.title: Your Challenge: Class Test Analysis
slides.storyContext: Class test scores: 45, 67, 78, 82, 55, 90, 73, 88, 60, 95. Find mean, median, standard deviation, and identify outliers.

example.problem: Analyze class test scores. Calculate mean, median, SD. Is 95 an outlier?
example.solution: Mean = 73.3. Sorted: 45,55,60,67,73,78,82,88,90,95. Median = 75.5. Using SD formula: σ ≈ 14.3. Using 3-sigma rule, 95 is within 3σ (73.3 + 3×14.3 = 116.2), so NOT a statistical outlier, but it's the highest score.

slides.inSimpleWords: Outliers are data points far from the mean—identify them using standard deviation.

slides.title: Statistics Summary

points.text: Mean (average), Median (middle), Mode (most frequent) are central tendencies.
Range, Variance, Standard Deviation measure data spread—lower SD = tighter clustering.
Frequency tables and histograms organize and visualize grouped data.
Cumulative frequency and quartiles divide data into parts; IQR measures middle 50%.
Correlation (r) measures relationship strength between two variables.
Statistics powers real decisions: health surveys, crop planning, quality control, market research.

slides.inSimpleWords: Statistics transforms raw numbers into insights—mean, median, spread, and patterns reveal the story in data.

subject: Mathematics
title: The Game of Chance
hook: Rolling dice, drawing cards, cricket match predictions—probability measures the likelihood of outcomes.

characters.name: Aunt Savita
characters.role: Mathematics teacher with a knack for games

characters.name: Zara
characters.role: Younger cousin exploring probability through card games

slides.title: Probability: Measuring Chance and Likelihood
slides.storyContext: Arjun commentates a cricket match. 'The batsman has a 60% chance of hitting a six on this ball,' he says. How do we calculate such odds?
slides.inSimpleWords: Probability measures how likely an event is to happen—from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

slides.title: The Card Game Night
slides.storyContext: Aunt Savita gathers Arjun and Zara for a game. 'Here's a standard deck of 52 cards. If I draw one card, what's the chance it's a heart?' Zara thinks: 'There are 13 hearts, so 13/52 = 1/4 = 25%.' Aunt nods. 'Exactly! The probability is 0.25. Now let's explore the rules of probability.' Arjun adds: 'Can we predict cricket match outcomes?' Aunt smiles: 'We'll get there. First, master the basics.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Probability = (favorable outcomes) / (total possible outcomes).

slides.title: Sample Space and Events

points.label: Sample Space (S)
points.text: Set of all possible outcomes. For a die: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. |S| = 6.

points.label: Event
points.text: Subset of sample space. Getting an even number: E = {2, 4, 6}. |E| = 3.

points.label: Probability of Event
points.text: P(E) = |E| / |S| = 3/6 = 0.5. Probability ranges from 0 to 1.

example.problem: A spinner has 8 equal sections: 4 red, 2 blue, 2 green. Find P(red) and P(not red).

slides.inSimpleWords: Sample space lists all outcomes; an event is a subset. Probability is favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.

slides.title: Classical and Empirical Probability

points.label: Classical Probability
points.text: Used when outcomes are equally likely. P(E) = (# favorable) / (# possible).

points.label: Empirical Probability
points.text: Based on experiments: P(E) = (# times event occurred) / (# total trials). Used when classical method is hard.

points.label: Example
points.text: Toss a coin 100 times: heads appear 52 times. Empirical P(heads) = 52/100 = 0.52 (close to theoretical 0.5).

example.problem: A cricket batsman hits 40 sixes in 200 balls. Estimate P(six on next ball).

slides.inSimpleWords: Classical probability uses logic; empirical probability uses real data from experiments.

slides.title: Rules of Probability: Addition and Multiplication

points.label: Addition Rule (OR)
points.text: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). For mutually exclusive events: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

points.label: Multiplication Rule (AND)
points.text: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A), where P(B|A) is conditional probability of B given A.

points.label: Independent Events
points.text: If A and B are independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

example.problem: Draw a card, note it, put it back (draw with replacement). What's P(both hearts)?
example.solution: P(1st heart) = 13/52 = 1/4. P(2nd heart | 1st heart) = 13/52 = 1/4 (independent). P(both hearts) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.

slides.inSimpleWords: Addition for 'or' (combine probabilities); multiplication for 'and' (successive events).

slides.title: Conditional Probability

points.label: Definition
points.text: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Probability of A given that B has already happened.

points.label: Card Example
points.text: From a deck, draw a card without replacement. P(2nd is heart | 1st is heart) = 12/51 (only 12 hearts left out of 51 cards).

points.label: Bayes' Theorem
points.text: P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B). Used to revise probabilities with new information.

example.problem: In a class, 60% pass Math, 80% pass Science, 50% pass both. Find P(pass Science | pass Math).

slides.inSimpleWords: Conditional probability updates likelihood when new information is given—vital for decision-making.

slides.title: Random Variables and Probability Distribution

points.label: Random Variable (X)
points.text: A function mapping outcomes to numbers. Example: rolling a die, X = number showing. X ∈ {1,2,3,4,5,6}.

points.label: Probability Distribution
points.text: Table/function showing P(X = x) for each outcome. For a fair die: P(X=1)=P(X=2)=...=P(X=6)=1/6.

points.label: Expected Value (Mean)
points.text: E(X) = Σ x × P(X=x). Average outcome over many trials. For a die: E(X) = 1/6 × (1+2+3+4+5+6) = 3.5.

example.problem: A game: roll a die, win ₹10 if even, lose ₹5 if odd. Find expected value.

slides.inSimpleWords: Random variables assign numbers to outcomes; expected value is the long-run average.

slides.title: Full Problem: The Cricket Match
slides.storyContext: Arjun predicts: a batsman hits 3 sixes per 20 balls on average. In the next 3 balls, what's the probability he hits exactly 2 sixes?
slides.inSimpleWords: Binomial probability calculates outcomes in repeated trials—useful for sports, quality control, surveys.

slides.title: Your Challenge: The Lottery
slides.storyContext: A lottery draws 1 winning ticket from 1,000. You buy 5 tickets. What's the probability of winning at least one prize?

example.problem: Find P(at least 1 win out of 5 tickets from 1000).

slides.inSimpleWords: For 'at least one' problems, calculate the complement: P(at least 1) = 1 - P(none).

slides.title: Probability Summary

points.text: Probability P(E) = (favorable outcomes) / (total outcomes). Range: 0 to 1.
Sample space = all outcomes. Event = subset of sample space.
Addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).
Multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A).
Conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B).
Random variables map outcomes to numbers; expected value is the average over many trials.
Applications: gambling, weather forecasting, quality control, medical diagnosis, sports analytics.

slides.inSimpleWords: Probability is the mathematics of uncertainty—used to predict outcomes and make informed decisions under risk.
